answer.label: Not Zig Ziglar — a marketing adage decades older than his version
answer.sourceLine: This is a classic sales-and-marketing adage, not a Zig Ziglar original. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the “drill vs. hole” idea to at least 1942 and its popular forms to Leo McGivena (via Percy Whiting, 1947) and Theodore Levitt (1969), who himself credited McGivena. The exact wording here — “People don’t want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole” — is Clayton Christensen’s 2005 phrasing, usually pinned on Levitt. Ziglar used a different version (“nobody wants a quarter-inch drill…”) in 1985.

source.excerpt: People don’t want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole.
trail: 1942: the earliest documented form appears in a life-insurance talk by C.C. Wagner — “a million men bought quarter-inch drills… they wanted quarter-inch holes” — per Quote Investigator ↗.
1947 & 1969: Percy Whiting’s sales manual credited adman Leo McGivena, and Theodore Levitt repeated it in 1969 — also crediting McGivena, not himself (QI ↗).
1985: Zig Ziglar used a version in Secrets of Closing the Sale ↗, but decades after the adage was in circulation — and worded differently.
2005: the exact modern wording is Clayton Christensen’s HBR phrasing, which fixed it in the popular mind as a “Levitt” line (Wikiquote ↗).
source.excerptNote: The canonical wording as it circulates today — Clayton Christensen’s 2005 phrasing, typically credited to Theodore Levitt. Ziglar’s own 1985 line read: “nobody wants a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole.”

author.metaLine: 1925–2006 · Harvard Business School economist who coined ‘marketing myopia’
author.bio: Theodore Levitt was a German-born American economist and longtime Harvard Business School professor, editor of the Harvard Business Review, and author of the landmark 1960 article “Marketing Myopia.” He popularized the idea that customers buy benefits, not products — and repeated the drill/hole illustration in 1969, though he credited it to adman Leo McGivena rather than claiming it himself.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: The line is a shared piece of sales-and-marketing folklore, not any one person’s coinage — and definitely not Zig Ziglar’s. Attribution has drifted across at least five names in eighty years.

items.why: Ziglar is a magnet for feel-good sales lines, but per Quote Investigator ↗ the adage was already decades old when he used a different version (“nobody wants a quarter-inch drill…”) in his 1985 book. He restated a classic; he didn’t originate it.

Marketing courses pin the exact wording on Levitt — but when Levitt used it in 1969 he credited Leo McGivena, per QI ↗. The neat “People don’t want to buy…” phrasing is actually Clayton Christensen’s 2005 rendering of Levitt.

Adman Leo McGivena is the earliest named source (via Percy Whiting, 1947), while the earliest documented wording of all is a 1942 life-insurance talk by C.C. Wagner — and QI ↗ notes it likely circulated even earlier.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: an anonymous sales adage documented from at least 1942, popularized by McGivena and Levitt — the exact modern wording is Christensen’s (2005), and Zig Ziglar is a late borrower, not the author (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The saying endures because it captures a genuine marketing insight in one image: a customer’s real goal is the outcome (the hole), not the tool (the drill). That framing became the seed of Theodore Levitt’s “marketing myopia” and, later, Clayton Christensen’s “jobs to be done” theory.

Because it is proverb-shaped and endlessly quotable, it detached from its murky origins and got re-credited to whoever a given reader admires — Levitt in business schools, Zig Ziglar in sales-training circles. That drift is exactly why its true, shared lineage is worth pinning down.
context.pull: Nobody wanted the drill. They wanted the hole — and nobody quite owns the sentence.
